title: Your First FastAPI Project
summary: See what FastAPI and Python are good at, install uv and Python, create Roombook's project, answer your first request, and learn how one loop serves many.
intro: The opening lessons looked at APIs from the outside: requests, responses, and the styles they come in. Now you build one. Before Roombook can answer a single request, you need the right tools on your computer, a project that anyone on your team can install the same way, folders with room to grow, and a server that starts with one command and reloads when you save. You'll repeat this setup at the start of every project, and when it's wrong, nothing after it works. This lesson covers what FastAPI and Python are good at, installing uv and Python, creating the project, what each file is for, your first route answering curl, and how FastAPI serves many people at once.

steps.title: What FastAPI and Python are good for
steps.body:
Every API is built on a **stack**: a language, the program that runs it, and a framework on top. Knowing what yours does well tells you which jobs it suits, and which problems you'll have to plan around. This course's stack is Python, with FastAPI on top, and three helpers you'll meet by name.

## Python runs your code

You know Python from your language course. The program that runs it is the **interpreter**, CPython, the `python` command. A program that runs code written in a language is called a **runtime**, so CPython is Python's runtime. On a server, it runs the same way it does on your laptop: one process, reading your files and running them.

## The pieces of a FastAPI app

A FastAPI app is a stack of its own, and each layer has one job:

- **Uvicorn** is the **server**: the program that listens on a port, reads the raw HTTP bytes from each connection, and writes the answers back.
- **ASGI**, the Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface, is the agreement between a Python server and a Python app: how the server hands over a request, and how the app hands back a response. Because it's a standard, any ASGI server can run any ASGI app. The older standard, **WSGI**, is the one Flask and classic Django use, and it can't wait on many things at once the way ASGI can.
- **Starlette** is the ASGI toolkit underneath FastAPI. It does the HTTP work: matching routes, reading requests, and writing responses.
- **Pydantic** checks and converts data using Python's type hints. You describe the shape of a booking once, and Pydantic turns incoming JSON into a Python object, or explains exactly what's wrong with it.
- **FastAPI** ties them together. Recall from the web course that you call a library, and a framework calls you. You write a function, tell FastAPI which method and path it handles, and FastAPI calls it when a matching request arrives. That function is a **handler**, and a method and a path that lead to one handler make a **route**.

The first example below shows what's left when you take FastAPI away: a bare ASGI app, talking to Uvicorn directly.

## What this stack is good at

- **Type hints do three jobs.** One declaration, like `room_id: int`, makes FastAPI convert the text in the URL to a number, reject a request when it isn't one, and describe the parameter in the API's documentation. You write less code, and the docs can't drift from it.
- **Docs from the first minute.** FastAPI builds an **OpenAPI** document, a standard description of every route, which the lesson on curl, Postman, and OpenAPI covers, and serves an interactive page at `/docs` where you can try each route in the browser.
- **APIs that mostly wait.** A typical request spends most of its time waiting: on the database, on another service, on the network. That's called **I/O-bound** work, I/O being short for input and output. Python's `async` and `await` let one process wait on many things at once, and the last part of this lesson shows how.
- **Python's libraries.** Data analysis, machine learning, and scientific computing live in Python, so an API that serves a model's predictions or crunches a report is often easiest to write here.
- **Fast to write.** Python is short and readable, which matters most when a team changes an API every week.

## Where it's weak

- **Raw speed.** Python runs slower than Go or Java, so the same server answers fewer requests per second. For most APIs the database is the bottleneck, not the language, but it adds up at large scale.
- **Heavy computing.** One process can run only one thread of Python at a time, because of a lock called the GIL, which the last part explains. Computing-heavy work needs more processes, or another service.
- **Types aren't checked when the code runs.** Pydantic checks data at the edges, but Python itself never checks your type hints, so a type checker is a separate tool you choose to run.

## Its neighbors

You'll hear about other Python frameworks. **Django** comes with everything, from a database layer to an admin site, and with Django REST Framework it builds APIs too. **Flask** is small and older, built on WSGI. **Litestar** is close to FastAPI in spirit. What you learn here carries over to all of them, since they answer the same HTTP requests in much the same way.

examples.title: One route with bare ASGI
examples.prompt: An ASGI app with no framework, answering `GET /healthz` with a little JSON and everything else with 404. You don't need to save this: it shows what FastAPI takes off your hands.
examples.explanation: Uvicorn calls `app` once per request. `scope` describes the request, a dictionary with its method, path, and headers, and `send` writes the answer in two messages: the status and headers, then the body. Everything is bytes, so the code encodes the JSON and the header values itself, and counts the body's length by hand. A second route means another `if`, and a path like `/v1/rooms/3` means cutting the 3 out of the path and checking that it's a number. Real APIs have dozens of routes, so this grows long and easy to get wrong.

examples.title: The same route with FastAPI
examples.prompt: The same API written with FastAPI.
examples.explanation: `FastAPI()` makes an app, which is itself an ASGI app that Uvicorn can run. The `@app.get("/healthz")` line is a **decorator**, a function written with `@` above another function that does something with it, and this one registers the function below as the handler for GET requests to `/healthz`. The handler returns a plain dictionary, and FastAPI turns it into JSON, sets the headers, and answers 404 by itself for any path that matches no route. The `-> dict[str, str]` is a return type hint, and FastAPI uses it to check and document what the route sends. The rest of this lesson builds Roombook's real version of this app.

steps.title: Installing uv and Python
steps.body:
Everything in this course runs on your own computer, in the Playground's terminal, so the first job is having the right tools there. Versions matter more than they look: code written for one version of Python can fail on an older one with errors that never mention the version, and a team loses an afternoon finding out why.

## uv: one tool for Python projects

Python's tools grew up separately: one installs Python, one makes isolated environments, one installs packages, one runs commands. **uv** does all of it, quickly, and it's what this course uses. It's made by Astral, the company behind Ruff, a code checker you'll add to the project in the next part.

Install it once, with the command for your system, from [docs.astral.sh/uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv). On a Mac or Linux:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

That downloads uv's install script with curl and runs it with `sh`, the shell. On Windows, in PowerShell:

```bash
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
```

If you use Homebrew on a Mac, `brew install uv` works too. Close and reopen the terminal afterwards, so it can find the new `uv` command.

## Python, through uv

Your computer may already have a Python, but it might be old, or belong to the operating system, which uses it for its own tools. uv installs the version a project needs, next to any others, and picks the right one for each project. This course uses **Python 3.14 or newer**:

```bash
uv python install 3.14
```

The first example shows what it prints. A new version of Python comes out every October, and each one gets fixes for five years, so 3.14, from October 2025, is good for years. Later versions run this course's code just as well.

## The terminal commands you'll use

The web course had you type a few commands. These are the ones every lesson from here on uses:

- `pwd` prints the folder the terminal is in, its **working directory**.
- `ls` lists what's in that folder.
- `mkdir roombook` makes a folder named roombook.
- `cd roombook` moves into it, and `cd ..` moves back up one level.
- **Ctrl+C** stops the program running in the terminal, like a server.
- The **Up arrow** brings back the last command, so you can run it again.

They work the same on a Mac and on Linux, and Windows PowerShell understands them too. Where a command differs on Windows, the lesson says so.

## Your editor

You can write the code in the Playground's editor, or in any editor you like. **VS Code** with Microsoft's **Python** extension is a common choice: it understands type hints, completes names, jumps to where a function is defined, and finds the project's environment by itself. **PyCharm** is the other popular one. Add the **Ruff** extension too, which underlines likely bugs as you type, using the same checker this lesson installs into the project.

examples.title: Checking uv, and installing Python
examples.prompt: Type these in the Playground's terminal, one at a time.
examples.output:
uv 0.13.9 (6b2d39dcc 2026-11-17 aarch64-apple-darwin)
Downloading cpython-3.14.10-macos-aarch64-none (download) (25.7MiB)

Installed Python 3.14.10 in 1.88s

examples.explanation: The first line is uv's version, 0.13.9, followed by the code revision it was built from, its release date, and the kind of computer it's built for: `aarch64-apple-darwin` is a Mac with an Apple chip. Then uv downloaded Python 3.14.10, the newest 3.14 release, and installed it in under two seconds. The three numbers are major, minor, and patch, and a patch release only fixes bugs. Your numbers will likely be higher, and your platform may differ, and that's fine, as long as Python is 3.14 or newer.

steps.title: Creating the project
steps.body:
A **project** is a folder of code plus a file that lists everything the code needs. With that list, anyone can rebuild the project on any computer with one command and get the same versions you have. Getting it right on day one is what saves a team from the oldest excuse in software: it works on my machine.

## Make the project

In the Playground's terminal:

```bash
uv init --app --no-package roombook
cd roombook
uv add "fastapi[standard]"
```

`uv init` makes the `roombook` folder and starts a project in it. `--app` says it's an application, a program you run, not a library for other projects to install. `--no-package` says uv runs the code where it is, without packaging it up first, which suits an API. uv also starts a Git repository in the folder.

`uv add` adds a **dependency**, a package the project needs, and installs it. `fastapi[standard]` is FastAPI plus its **extra** called `standard`: the pieces most apps want, including Uvicorn, the `fastapi` command, and the libraries for reading forms and sending files. The quotes stop the terminal from treating the brackets as a pattern of file names. uv prints the Python it chose, then one line per package it installed, 59 of them: you asked for one, and FastAPI depends on others, which depend on others.

## What uv made

- **pyproject.toml** is the project's own description, the Python world's version of the `package.json` you met in the web course: its name, the Python it needs, and its dependencies. The second example shows Roombook's.
- **uv.lock** is the **lockfile**. `pyproject.toml` says `fastapi[standard]>=0.165.0`, which allows any newer version, so two installs a month apart could get different code. The lockfile records the exact version of every package, so the next install matches. Commit it with your code. `uv sync --locked` installs exactly what it says, and it's what servers and automated builds use.
- **.venv** is the project's **virtual environment**: a folder with its own Python and its own installed packages, so two projects on one computer never fight over versions. Never commit it, and never edit it by hand: uv rebuilds it from the lockfile whenever it needs to.
- **.python-version** holds `3.14`, the Python uv uses for this project.
- **main.py** is a hello-world script, and **README.md** is empty. Delete `main.py`, since Roombook's code goes in a folder, as the next part shows.

## uv run

`uv run` runs a command inside the project's environment: `uv run python` is this project's Python, with this project's packages. Before it runs anything, it checks the environment against the lockfile and fixes any difference, so a teammate who pulls new code and types `uv run` gets the new packages without thinking about it. That's why you never need to **activate** the environment, the older way of switching a terminal into one.

## A tool just for development

Some tools help you write code but aren't part of the running API. They go in a **development group**:

```bash
uv add --dev ruff
```

**Ruff** reads your code for mistakes, like a name used before it's defined, and tidies its style. It's a **linter**, and it's very fast, since it's written in Rust. The first example shows the project's dependencies after this.

## Tell FastAPI where the app is

Last, add a section to `pyproject.toml` that says where Roombook's app lives, so the `fastapi` command never has to guess. The second example shows the whole file with it: `entrypoint = "app.main:app"` means the variable `app` in the module `app/main.py`.

examples.title: The project's dependencies
examples.prompt: `uv tree` prints what the project depends on, and `--depth 1` stops at the packages you added yourself.
examples.output:
Resolved 63 packages in 3ms
roombook v0.1.0
├── fastapi[standard] v0.165.0
└── ruff v0.17.6 (group: dev)
examples.explanation: uv first checked that the lockfile still matches `pyproject.toml`, which means resolving 63 packages: a few more than it installed, since the lockfile covers every system, including packages only Windows needs. Then it drew the tree. Roombook depends on FastAPI 0.165 with its standard extra, and on Ruff 0.17.6, marked as part of the `dev` group, so a production install can leave it out with `uv sync --no-dev`. FastAPI's version still starts with 0, even though it's stable and widely used, and new 0.x releases do sometimes change behavior, which is one more reason to commit the lockfile. Run `uv tree` without `--depth` to see all 59 packages and who needs each one.

examples.title: Roombook's pyproject.toml
examples.prompt: The whole file after `uv add` and your edit, at the top of the `roombook` folder. The version numbers are the ones uv installed here, and yours may be newer.
examples.code:
[project]
name = "roombook"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "fastapi[standard]>=0.165.0",
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "ruff>=0.17.6",
]

[tool.fastapi]
entrypoint = "app.main:app"
examples.explanation: This is **TOML**, a format for settings files: `[project]` starts a section, and each line below sets one value. `requires-python` says the project needs Python 3.14 or newer, and uv refuses to run it on anything older. `dependencies` lists what the API needs to run, and `uv add` wrote that line for you, with the version it installed as the minimum. `[dependency-groups]` holds the `dev` group, and `[tool.fastapi]` is a section for the `fastapi` command. Other tools keep their settings here too, like Ruff and pytest in later lessons, so one file configures the whole project.

steps.title: The project's files and folders
steps.body:
Where code lives decides how fast you can find it and how safely you can change it. A good layout puts each feature's code together, so a change to bookings happens in one folder, and keeps the code that builds the app apart from the code that answers requests, which is what makes the API easy to test. Roombook starts small, but its layout is planned for everything the course adds.

```diagram first-project-tree
Today the project holds settings files and one source file. Each later lesson adds a file or a folder.
```

## The app package

Roombook's code lives in a folder named `app`. A folder with a file named `__init__.py` in it is a Python **package**, recall from your language course, and its files are **modules** you can import by name: `app/main.py` is the module `app.main`, and later `app/rooms/router.py` is `app.rooms.router`. `__init__.py` can stay empty. Make both now: the folder, and an empty `app/__init__.py`.

## main.py: create_app and app

`app/main.py` holds two things, and the split between them is deliberate.

`create_app()` builds the FastAPI app: it adds the routes and everything else the app needs, and returns it, without starting a server. A function that builds and returns something ready to use is called a **factory**, so `create_app` is the **app factory**.

`app = create_app()`, the last line, builds one app when the module is imported. That variable is the **entry point**, where everything starts: it's what `fastapi dev` imports and hands to Uvicorn, and it's the `app.main:app` in `pyproject.toml`.

Why both? Because tests, in the testing lesson, call `create_app()` to get a fresh app of their own for each test, and send requests straight to it in memory, with no port and no network. They can even swap in fake parts, like a database that lives in memory. That only works if building the app is a function you can call again, not just a variable made once.

## Folders by feature

As Roombook grows, each feature gets its own folder inside `app`: `rooms`, `bookings`, `auth` for logins, and `feedback`. Each holds the same kinds of file: `router.py` for its routes, `schemas.py` for the shapes of its JSON, and the files the lesson on services and repositories introduces for its rules and its data. Some projects group code by kind instead, with one `routers` folder, one `models` folder, and so on. That splits every feature across many folders, so one change touches all of them. Grouping by feature keeps a change in one place.

The rest of `app` holds what features share:

- `config.py` reads every setting from the environment and checks it when the app starts, so a typo in a setting stops the server at once instead of breaking a request hours later.
- `errors.py` and `problems.py` hold Roombook's errors and the one format it answers them in, which the lesson on validation and errors builds, and `deps.py` holds pieces that many routes ask for, like who's calling.
- `db.py` opens the connections to the databases, from the PostgreSQL lesson on.
- `worker.py` is a second entry point, for background jobs like sending emails, which the MongoDB and Redis lessons build.

Next to `app`, `migrations/` holds the files that set up the database, from the PostgreSQL lesson on, `scripts/` holds small tools that run them, and `tests/` holds the tests.

## Settings and secrets: .env

A setting that changes between computers, like the port or a database password, doesn't belong in the code. It goes in an **environment variable**, a named value the operating system hands a program when it starts. While you build, teams keep theirs in a file named `.env`, one `NAME=value` per line. Roombook doesn't need one yet, since its only setting, the port, has a good default. `config.py` starts reading one in a later lesson.

## What Git leaves out

`.gitignore` lists what Git, the tool that records versions of your code, should leave out, one pattern per line. uv wrote one, and the example shows it with one line added at the end. A `.env` file will hold passwords one day, and a password committed to Git stays in its history for good, even after you delete the file.

examples.title: Roombook's .gitignore
examples.prompt: uv wrote all but the last line. Add `.env` at the end yourself.
examples.code:
# Python-generated files
__pycache__/
*.py[oc]
build/
dist/
wheels/
*.egg-info

# Virtual environments
.venv
.env
examples.explanation: Each line is a pattern, and Git acts as if anything matching it isn't there. Lines starting with `#` are comments. `__pycache__/` is where Python saves compiled copies of your modules to start faster, and `*.py[oc]` matches those files wherever they are. `build/`, `dist/`, `wheels/`, and `*.egg-info` are what packaging tools make. `.venv` is there because uv can always rebuild it from the lockfile. Add a `.gitignore` before your first commit: once Git has recorded a file, adding it here afterwards doesn't remove it from the history.

steps.title: Your first endpoint: GET /healthz
steps.body:
Nearly every API has one route that only answers: yes, I'm up. The tools that run your API in production, like the load balancers in the lesson on scaling out, call it every few seconds, and stop sending traffic to a copy that doesn't answer. It's also the simplest route there is, so it proves the whole setup works before you write anything real. Roombook's is `GET /healthz`. The z is a habit from Google's servers, and it makes the path unlikely to clash with a real resource.

## app/main.py

Create `app/main.py`:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI


def create_app() -> FastAPI:
    app = FastAPI(title="Roombook API")

    @app.get("/healthz")
    async def healthz() -> dict[str, str]:
        return {"status": "ok"}

    return app


app = create_app()
```

`FastAPI(title=...)` makes the app, and the title shows at the top of its docs page. The route is registered inside `create_app`, so every app it makes has it. `async def` makes the handler a **coroutine function**, one that can pause while it waits for something, and the last part of this lesson explains when that matters. The next lesson covers routes in full.

## Run it

```bash
uv run fastapi dev
```

`fastapi dev` reads the entry point from `pyproject.toml`, imports `app.main`, and starts Uvicorn with **reload** on: it watches your files, and when you save one, it restarts the app with your change. It keeps running, and holds the terminal, until you press Ctrl+C. The first example shows what it prints.

`fastapi dev` listens on `127.0.0.1`, loopback, recall from the web course: only programs on your own computer can connect, which is what you want while you build. Its port comes from the environment variable `PORT`, and it's 8000 when that isn't set. To use another port for a moment, set the variable in front of the command:

```bash
PORT=9000 uv run fastapi dev
```

In Windows PowerShell, write `$env:PORT=9000; uv run fastapi dev` instead. For production, `fastapi run` starts the same app without reload, listening on `0.0.0.0` so other machines can reach it, which the deployment lesson comes back to. If the port is already taken, often by an earlier copy of this server in another terminal, Uvicorn stops with `ERROR: [Errno 48] Address already in use`, even though FastAPI's banner above it already said the server started. The 48 is macOS's number for this error, and Linux uses 98. Stop that one with Ctrl+C, or pick another port.

## Ask it with curl

The Playground's terminal is busy running the server, so send requests from a second one: your computer's own terminal, as in the web course, like Terminal on a Mac. The second example sends the request. Then try a path Roombook doesn't have yet:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:8000/v1/rooms
```

FastAPI answers `404 Not Found` with a small JSON body, `{"detail":"Not Found"}`. That's FastAPI's own shape for errors, and the next lesson gives Roombook's errors a shape of their own.

## Docs, already

Open `http://localhost:8000/docs` in your browser. FastAPI built a page that lists every route, here just `/healthz`, and lets you send a request with its **Try it out** button. It's drawn from the OpenAPI document at `/openapi.json`:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8000/openapi.json
```

```text
{"openapi":"3.1.0","info":{"title":"Roombook API","version":"0.1.0"},"paths":{"/healthz":{"get":{"summary":"Healthz","operationId":"healthz_healthz_get","responses":{"200":{"description":"Successful Response","content":{"application/json":{"schema":{"additionalProperties":{"type":"string"},"type":"object","title":"Response Healthz Healthz Get"}}}}}}}}}
```

Every route you add shows up there by itself, with its parameters and the shape of its answer, which the OpenAPI lesson builds on.

## Check the code

Python only finds some mistakes when the line runs. Write `{"status": ok}`, forgetting the quotes, and `fastapi dev` starts without a complaint: the error, a `NameError`, waits until the first request reaches that line, and that request gets a 500. `uv run ruff check` finds it first, as the third example shows. Run it before you commit, and the testing lesson makes the automated builds run it too. A **type checker**, like mypy, goes further and checks that your values match your type hints, and many teams add one.

examples.title: Calling GET /healthz
examples.prompt: From your computer's own terminal, with the server still running in the Playground. `-i` makes curl print the response's status line and headers before the body.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:54:34 GMT
server: uvicorn
content-length: 15
content-type: application/json

{"status":"ok"}
examples.explanation: The status is `200 OK`, and FastAPI turned the dictionary into JSON, with `content-type: application/json` and `content-length` set to the body's 15 bytes. Uvicorn writes header names in lowercase, which is fine, since recall from the web course that header names ignore capital letters. `server: uvicorn` names the server program to anyone who asks, which mostly helps attackers know what to try, and the security lesson deals with headers like that. There's no `ETag` header, a fingerprint of the body that some frameworks add by themselves, and the lesson on request data adds one where it helps.

examples.title: A mistake Ruff catches
examples.prompt: Change `"ok"` to `ok`, without the quotes, in `app/main.py`. Then run the checker, and change it back afterwards.

  --> app/main.py:9:27

   |                           ^^
10 |
11 |     return app

Found 1 error.
examples.explanation: Ruff names the rule first, `F821`, and what's wrong: a name that's used but never defined. Then it shows where, `app/main.py`, line 9, column 27, with the lines around it and carets under the exact spot. Meanwhile `fastapi dev` kept running and reported nothing, since the line only fails when it runs. With the quotes back, `uv run ruff check` prints `All checks passed!`. `uv run ruff format` also tidies the code's layout, so a team never argues about spacing.

steps.title: How FastAPI handles many requests
steps.body:
Roombook will have hundreds of students checking rooms at the same moment. How a framework serves many requests at once decides how fast your API is under load, and which mistakes slow everyone down. FastAPI does it with an **event loop**, and one wrong line can stall it for everyone.

## Processes and threads

A **process** is a running program with its own memory: `fastapi dev` starts one for your app. A **thread** is one line of work inside a process, running one instruction after another. A process can have many threads, and a computer has several **cores**, the parts of its processor that each run one thread at a time.

## The event loop

A request mostly waits, recall the I/O-bound work from the first part. So instead of giving each request a thread, Uvicorn runs an **event loop**: a loop on one thread that juggles many requests. Each `async def` handler is a **coroutine**, a function that can pause. When it reaches an `await`, like `await` on a database query, it pauses there, and the loop runs another request's coroutine until that one pauses too. When the query's answer arrives, the loop picks the first coroutine up again, right after its `await`.

```diagram first-project-runtime
One loop runs the async handlers, threads run the plain ones, and workers use more cores.
```

Follow the steps in the diagram:

1. The loop runs request A's handler until it reaches an `await`.
2. While A waits, the loop runs B, then C, each until its next `await`. A thousand waiting requests cost the loop almost nothing.
3. A handler written with plain `def`, not `async def`, can't pause, so FastAPI runs it on a **thread pool**, a set of threads kept ready, 40 by default. The loop stays free while it runs.
4. More **worker processes**, each with its own loop, serve requests side by side, as the end of this part explains.

## The one rule: never block the loop

Here's the catch. A coroutine only gives up the loop at an `await`. If an `async def` handler does something slow without awaiting, every other request waits behind it, even a health check. That's called **blocking the event loop**, and the examples show it happen. Things that block:

- `time.sleep()`, where `await asyncio.sleep()` was meant.
- Libraries that wait without `await`, like `requests` for HTTP calls or a database driver that isn't async. Use their async versions, like `httpx2`, or the async driver the PostgreSQL lesson sets up.
- Long loops over lots of data, and heavy math.

So the rule is: inside `async def`, only fast code and `await`. If you must call something slow that can't be awaited, write that handler with plain `def`, and FastAPI runs it on the thread pool instead.

## The GIL

Threads have a limit in Python. The **GIL**, the Global Interpreter Lock, lets only one thread run Python code at a time in a process. A thread that's waiting, on a file, the network, or `time.sleep`, lets go of it, so threads help with waiting. They don't help with computing: two threads crunching numbers take turns, not cores. Python 3.14 also ships a **free-threaded** build, named `python3.14t`, that drops the GIL, but it's optional, and many libraries aren't ready for it yet.

## Workers: one process per core

So one process runs Python on about one core. To use all eight cores of a server, you run several processes: `fastapi run --workers 8` starts eight worker processes, each with its own loop, its own memory, and its own GIL. The lesson on scaling out does this, and explains what it means for anything a worker keeps in memory. Until then, one process is plenty: even on a laptop, it answers thousands of small requests a second.

The next lesson gives Roombook its real routes: rooms and bookings, every HTTP method, and the status code that goes with each answer.

examples.title: Three ways to wait two seconds
examples.prompt: A demo, not part of Roombook: save it as `blocking.py` next to `pyproject.toml`, and run it with `uv run fastapi dev blocking.py` after stopping the dev server.
examples.explanation: All three slow routes take two seconds to answer, but they spend them differently. `/blocking` calls `time.sleep` inside `async def`, so it holds the event loop for the whole two seconds. `/waiting` awaits `asyncio.sleep`, which pauses the coroutine and hands the loop back. `/threaded` calls the same `time.sleep`, but in a plain `def`, so FastAPI runs it on the thread pool, and the loop never notices. The next example times a health check while each one runs. Delete the file when you're done, since it isn't part of Roombook.

examples.title: Timing a health check behind each one
examples.prompt: In your computer's own terminal, each block starts a slow request in the background, waits a tenth of a second, then times a call to /healthz. `-w` prints the time, and `-o /dev/null` hides the body.
examples.code:
(curl -s localhost:8000/blocking > /dev/null &)
sleep 0.1
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "healthz answered in %{time_total}s\n" localhost:8000/healthz

(curl -s localhost:8000/waiting > /dev/null &)
sleep 0.1
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "healthz answered in %{time_total}s\n" localhost:8000/healthz

(curl -s localhost:8000/threaded > /dev/null &)
sleep 0.1
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "healthz answered in %{time_total}s\n" localhost:8000/healthz
examples.output:
healthz answered in 1.899509s
healthz answered in 0.000734s
healthz answered in 0.001062s
examples.explanation: The `&` runs the first curl in the background, and the parentheses keep the terminal from printing a note about it. Behind `/blocking`, the health check took 1.9 seconds: it waited for `time.sleep` to finish, minus the tenth of a second head start. Behind `/waiting` and `/threaded`, it took under a millisecond, since the loop was free. Same two seconds, very different effects on everyone else. Wait for each slow request to finish before you start the next block, or the timings mix.

recap:
- Uvicorn is the server, ASGI is how it talks to the app, Starlette does the HTTP work, Pydantic checks data, and FastAPI ties them together.
- Type hints drive FastAPI: they convert and check each value, and fill in the docs at /docs.
- uv installs Python, makes the project's .venv, adds packages, and runs commands with uv run.
- pyproject.toml lists the dependencies and uv.lock pins every exact version: commit both, and never commit .venv.
- app/main.py has create_app(), the app factory, and app, the entry point that fastapi dev imports.
- fastapi dev reloads on save and listens on 127.0.0.1, on PORT from the environment or 8000.
- Ruff catches mistakes Python only finds when a line runs, so run uv run ruff check before you commit.
- An async def handler must never block the loop, plain def handlers run on a thread pool, and more workers use more cores.
